fields.Notes: The standard way of conveying speed in sports and motor photography.
fields.Description: Swinging the camera with a moving subject during a long exposure so it stays sharp while the background streaks.
fields.Captions: A running chicken, panned at 1/40 second | A racing car, panned at 1/80 second

fields.Title: Camera obscura
fields.Notes: Known since antiquity and used as a drawing aid for centuries before anyone could fix its image.
fields.Description: A darkened room or box with a small hole that projects an inverted image of the scene outside onto the opposite surface.
fields.Captions: The street outside projected upside down inside Wat Thong Laplae, Thailand | Prague Castle's New Royal Palace projected in a darkened room

fields.Title: Pinhole photography
fields.Notes: The simplest possible camera, and the direct descendant of the darkened room.
fields.Description: Making an image with a tiny aperture and no lens at all, giving infinite depth of field and very long exposures.
fields.Captions: A pinhole camera | A fire hydrant exposed straight onto paper through a pinhole

fields.Title: Contact sheet
fields.Notes: The photographer's editing tool; Magnum's are studied as documents of how pictures were chosen.
fields.Description: A single page carrying every frame of a roll at negative size, laid out together for selection.
fields.Captions: Contact sheets of cut strips of negatives | A contact sheet from 35 mm film

fields.Title: Bracketing
fields.Notes: Standard insurance before instant review of results was possible.
fields.Description: Making several exposures of one subject at different settings to guarantee that one is correct.
fields.Captions: Three bracketed exposures: under, correct, and over

fields.Title: Rule of thirds
fields.Notes: A convention inherited from painting, as often broken deliberately as followed.
fields.Description: Composing by placing the main subject on one of the lines dividing the frame into nine equal parts.
fields.Captions: A photograph divided by the rule-of-thirds grid | A walker placed where the frame's thirds intersect

fields.Title: Bokeh
fields.Notes: From the Japanese for blur; determined by the shape of the aperture and the design of the lens.
fields.Description: The visual quality of the out-of-focus areas of an image, as distinct from how much of it is unsharp.
fields.Captions: Out-of-focus candle flames | A portrait with bokeh behind the sitter | The same scene at f/1.4 and at f/22

fields.Title: Pictorialism
fields.Notes: Dominant around 1900; the Photo-Secession was its American vehicle.
fields.Description: An approach insisting photography was an art by making prints that looked handmade: soft focus, brush-marked surfaces, allegorical subjects.
fields.Captions: Alfred Stieglitz, Spring Showers, the Coach, 1899–1900 | George Seeley, The Black Bowl, 1907 | Eva Watson-Schütze, The Rose, 1905

fields.Title: Straight photography
fields.Notes: Paul Strand's 1917 Camera Work issue is the turning point; Edward Weston and Adams carried it on.
fields.Description: A reaction against handworked prints, insisting on sharp focus, full tonal range, and no manipulation.
fields.Captions: Paul Strand, Wall Street, 1915

fields.Title: Group f/64
fields.Notes: Named for the smallest aperture then marked; Adams, Edward Weston, Imogen Cunningham, and Van Dyke were members.
fields.Description: A West Coast association of the 1930s committed to maximum sharpness front to back and to unmanipulated printing.
fields.Captions: Ansel Adams, Half Dome, Apple Orchard, Yosemite, 1933

fields.Title: New Objectivity
fields.Notes: Neue Sachlichkeit. The photographic strand is Renger-Patzsch, Blossfeldt, and August Sander; the painting movement of the same name is Dix, Grosz, and Beckmann.
fields.Description: A German interwar manner of cool, close, frontal description, treating plants and machines with the same detachment.
fields.Captions: Karl Blossfeldt, plant study, 1920s

fields.Title: The decisive moment
fields.Notes: Henri Cartier-Bresson's phrase, from the title of his 1952 book.
fields.Description: The idea that a photograph succeeds when form and event coincide for a fraction of a second, and that the photographer's job is to recognize it.
fields.Captions: Henri Cartier-Bresson, Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare, 1932 | Cartier-Bresson's first Leica

fields.Title: Photo-Secession
fields.Notes: Founded by Alfred Stieglitz in 1902; the journal was Camera Work and the gallery 291.
fields.Description: An American group formed to win recognition for photography as a fine art, with its own gallery and journal.
fields.Captions: Alfred Stieglitz, The Steerage, 1907 | Edward Steichen, The Flatiron, 1904

fields.Title: Farm Security Administration
fields.Notes: Roy Stryker directed it; Dorothea Lange, Evans, Parks, Rothstein, and Shahn all worked for it.
fields.Description: A United States government photographic unit documenting rural poverty in the Depression to build support for relief.
fields.Captions: Dorothea Lange, Migrant Mother, 1936 | Walker Evans, Allie Mae Burroughs, 1936 | Arthur Rothstein, Farmer and Sons Walking in the Face of a Dust Storm, 1936 | Lone Driller's Water Break, 1939

fields.Title: New Topographics
fields.Notes: Named for a 1975 exhibition; Robert Adams, Lewis Baltz, and the Bechers.
fields.Description: A 1970s turn toward deadpan, unpicturesque description of the built and altered landscape.
fields.Captions: George Eastman House, Rochester, which mounted the 1975 exhibition

fields.Title: Street photography
fields.Notes: Eugène Atget, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Frank, Garry Winogrand, Vivian Maier.
fields.Description: Unposed picture-making in public places, alert to chance juxtaposition and gesture.
fields.Captions: Louis Daguerre, Boulevard du Temple, 1838 | Charles Nègre, a water seller in Paris

fields.Title: Photojournalism
fields.Notes: Grew with the illustrated magazines: Life, Picture Post, and the Magnum cooperative.
fields.Description: Reporting news through photographs, generally in sequences laid out as a picture story.
fields.Captions: Joe Rosenthal, Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima, 1945 | Eugène Thibault, Barricades on rue Saint-Maur, 1848, among the first news photographs

fields.Title: Alfred Stieglitz
fields.Notes: The Steerage, Winter, Fifth Avenue, and the cloud series Equivalents; he photographed his wife, Georgia O'Keeffe, for twenty years.
fields.Description: He ran the gallery 291 and edited Camera Work to win photography a place among the fine arts.
fields.Captions: The Steerage, 1907 | Camera Work, 1903–1917 | Georgia O'Keeffe: A Portrait, 1918–1937

fields.Title: Dorothea Lange
fields.Notes: Migrant Mother and White Angel Breadline; her pictures of Japanese-American internment were impounded by the Army.
fields.Description: She photographed Florence Owens Thompson and her children at a pea pickers' camp in Nipomo, California.
fields.Captions: Migrant Mother, 1936 | White Angel Breadline, 1933 | Manzanar Relocation Center, 1942

fields.Title: Man Ray
fields.Notes: Born Emmanuel Radnitzky. Le Violon d'Ingres, Noire et blanche, and Larmes; he named his cameraless prints rayographs.
fields.Description: The American Surrealist in Paris who painted f-holes on a print of Kiki de Montparnasse's back.
fields.Captions: Le Violon d'Ingres, 1924 | Kiki with African Mask, 1926 | Larmes, 1930

fields.Title: Ansel Adams
fields.Notes: Monolith, the Face of Half Dome, Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico, and Clearing Winter Storm; a founder of Group f/64.
fields.Description: He devised the Zone System with Fred Archer, so that a print's tones could be planned before the exposure.
fields.Captions: Monolith, the Face of Half Dome, 1927 | Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico, 1941 | Clearing Winter Storm, c. 1937

fields.Title: Diane Arbus
fields.Notes: Child with Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park and A Jewish Giant at Home with His Parents in the Bronx; shown in the Museum of Modern Art's New Documents in 1967.
fields.Description: She photographed identical twin girls in matching corduroy dresses in Roselle, New Jersey.
fields.Captions: Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey, 1967 | Child with Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park, 1962 | A Jewish Giant at Home with His Parents in the Bronx, 1970

fields.Title: Margaret Bourke-White
fields.Notes: The first woman accredited as a war correspondent by the U.S. Army; she photographed the liberation of Buchenwald and Gandhi at his spinning wheel.
fields.Description: Her picture of the Fort Peck Dam was the cover of the first issue of Life.
fields.Captions: Buchenwald, 1945 | Fort Peck Dam, 1936 | Gandhi at His Spinning Wheel, 1946

fields.Title: Henri Cartier-Bresson
fields.Notes: Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare; he co-founded Magnum Photos in 1947 with Robert Capa, David Seymour, and George Rodger.
fields.Description: The title of the English edition of his 1952 book gave photography the phrase “the decisive moment”.
fields.Captions: Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare, 1932 | Juvisy, France, 1938

fields.Title: Robert Mapplethorpe
fields.Notes: Calla lilies, the X Portfolio, and portraits of Patti Smith, including the cover of Horses; he died of AIDS in 1989.
fields.Description: The cancellation of his retrospective The Perfect Moment at the Corcoran Gallery set off a fight over public arts funding.
fields.Captions: Self-Portrait, 1988 | Calla Lily, 1988 | Man in a Polyester Suit, 1980

fields.Title: Cindy Sherman
fields.Notes: Untitled #96, from the Centerfolds, set an auction record for a photograph in 2011; she belongs to the Pictures Generation.
fields.Description: She cast herself as the heroines of films that never existed in seventy black-and-white Untitled Film Stills.
fields.Captions: Untitled Film Stills, 1977–1980 | Untitled Film Still #21, 1978 | Untitled #96, 1981

fields.Title: Edward Steichen
fields.Notes: A Pictorialist in his youth (The Flatiron, The Pond—Moonlight) and Stieglitz's partner at 291; later chief photographer for Vogue and Vanity Fair.
fields.Description: He organized the Museum of Modern Art's The Family of Man, an exhibition of 503 photographs from 68 countries.
fields.Captions: The Flatiron, 1904 | The Family of Man, 1955 | The Pond—Moonlight, 1904

fields.Title: Walker Evans
fields.Notes: Allie Mae Burroughs; he hid a camera in his coat for his Subway Portraits, and American Photographs (1938) was the Museum of Modern Art's first solo show of a photographer.
fields.Description: He photographed three Alabama tenant-farming families for Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, with text by James Agee.
fields.Captions: Allie Mae Burroughs, 1936 | Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, 1941 | Penny Picture Display, 1936

fields.Title: Richard Avedon
fields.Notes: A Harper's Bazaar fashion photographer whose white-background portraits culminated in In the American West (1985).
fields.Description: He photographed the model Dovima in a Dior gown between two chained elephants at the Cirque d'Hiver.
fields.Captions: Dovima with Elephants, 1955 | Portrait of Richard Avedon

fields.Title: Annie Leibovitz
fields.Notes: Chief photographer of Rolling Stone, then of Vanity Fair, where she shot a pregnant Demi Moore for the cover.
fields.Description: She photographed a naked John Lennon curled around Yoko Ono hours before he was murdered.
fields.Captions: John Lennon and Yoko Ono, 1980 | More Demi Moore, 1991

fields.Title: Eadweard Muybridge
fields.Notes: The Horse in Motion (1878); his zoopraxiscope projected motion sequences, and he was acquitted of murdering his wife's lover.
fields.Description: Commissioned by Leland Stanford, he showed that a galloping horse has all four hooves off the ground at once.
fields.Captions: Attitudes of Animals in Motion, 1881

fields.Title: Edward Weston
fields.Notes: Pepper No. 30; a founder of Group f/64 and the first photographer to win a Guggenheim Fellowship. His Daybooks record his years in Mexico with Tina Modotti.
fields.Description: He photographed a single green pepper set inside a tin funnel.
fields.Captions: Pepper No. 30, 1930 | Armco Steel, 1922 | Tide Pool, Point Lobos, 1945

fields.Title: Nadar
fields.Notes: Born Gaspard-Félix Tournachon; he took the first aerial photographs from a balloon, and portraits of Baudelaire, Sarah Bernhardt, and Victor Hugo.
fields.Description: The Parisian caricaturist whose former studio held the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874.
fields.Captions: Sarah Bernhardt, 1864 | The Mime Charles Deburau as Pierrot, 1854

fields.Title: Gordon Parks
fields.Notes: The first Black staff photographer at Life; he wrote The Learning Tree and directed Shaft (1971).
fields.Description: His American Gothic, Washington, D.C. shows a government cleaner with her mop and broom before the flag.
fields.Captions: American Gothic, Washington, D.C., 1942 | Flavio da Silva, 1961

fields.Title: Robert Capa
fields.Notes: Born Endre Friedmann; his D-Day pictures survive as The Magnificent Eleven. A co-founder of Magnum, he was killed by a landmine in Indochina.
fields.Description: His picture of a Republican militiaman at the instant of being shot made his name in the Spanish Civil War.
fields.Captions: The Magnificent Eleven, 1944 | The Falling Soldier, 1936

fields.Title: Julia Margaret Cameron
fields.Notes: A Victorian amateur on the Isle of Wight, whose blur was dismissed as incompetence; Virginia Woolf was her great-niece.
fields.Description: She took up photography at forty-eight and made soft-focus portraits of Herschel, Tennyson, and Darwin.
fields.Captions: Call, I Follow, I Follow, Let Me Die!, 1867 | Portrait of Sir John Herschel, 1867

fields.Title: Nan Goldin
fields.Notes: Nan One Month After Being Battered; she later led protests against the Sackler family, the subject of All the Beauty and the Bloodshed (2022).
fields.Description: Her slide show The Ballad of Sexual Dependency records her friends and lovers in 1980s New York.
fields.Captions: The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, 1986 | Nan One Month After Being Battered, 1984

fields.Title: Imogen Cunningham
fields.Notes: Magnolia Blossom and Two Callas; she was still photographing in her nineties, collected in After Ninety.
fields.Description: A founder of Group f/64 known for close studies of magnolias and calla lilies.
fields.Captions: Magnolia Blossom, 1925 | Two Callas, 1929

fields.Title: Weegee
fields.Notes: Born Arthur Fellig; his photographs were collected in Naked City (1945).
fields.Description: The New York crime photographer who kept a police radio in his car and took his name from the Ouija board.
fields.Captions: The Critic, 1943 | Mulberry Street, 1939

fields.Title: Louis Daguerre
fields.Notes: Boulevard du Temple (1838) holds the first people ever photographed; he had worked with Nicéphore Niépce until Niépce's death.
fields.Description: The scene painter and Diorama owner whose process on silvered copper plates was announced in Paris in 1839.
fields.Captions: Boulevard du Temple, 1838 | The Artist's Studio, 1837

fields.Title: Paul Strand
fields.Notes: Wall Street and Abstraction, Porch Shadows filled the last issue of Camera Work (1917), the turn to straight photography.
fields.Description: He photographed a blind woman with a sign around her neck, using a false lens so that she would not know.
fields.Captions: Wall Street, 1915 | Blind Woman, New York, 1916 | Abstraction Porch Shadows, 1916

fields.Title: Brassaï
fields.Notes: Born Gyula Halász, he took his name from his home town, Brassó; Henry Miller called him “the eye of Paris”.
fields.Description: The Hungarian-born photographer of Paris's night streets and brothels in Paris de nuit.
fields.Captions: Paris by Night, 1933

fields.Title: Andreas Gursky
fields.Notes: Rhein II and 99 Cent II Diptychon; he studied with Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Düsseldorf Academy.
fields.Description: His digitally simplified view of a grey river between strips of grass sold for $4.3 million in 2011.
fields.Captions: 99 Cent II Diptychon, 2001 | Rhein II, 1999

fields.Title: Lee Miller
fields.Notes: Man Ray's assistant and partner in Paris, with whom she worked out solarization; the bathtub picture was taken by David E. Scherman.
fields.Description: The Vogue war correspondent who posed in Hitler's bathtub in Munich on the day he died.
fields.Captions: Lee Miller with her camera in London, 1943, as a U.S. Army war correspondent

fields.Title: Robert Frank
fields.Notes: A Swiss immigrant on a Guggenheim grant; Trolley—New Orleans is on its cover. He later made the Beat film Pull My Daisy.
fields.Description: His road-trip book The Americans appeared in France first, then in the United States with an introduction by Jack Kerouac.
fields.Captions: Trolley—New Orleans, 1955

fields.Title: Mathew Brady
fields.Notes: He sent photographers, among them Alexander Gardner and Timothy O'Sullivan, to cover the Civil War, and showed The Dead of Antietam in New York.
fields.Description: His portrait of Lincoln, made the day of the Cooper Union speech in 1860, was said to have helped make him president.
fields.Captions: Abraham Lincoln, 1860 | Portrait of Mathew Brady

fields.Title: Jacob Riis
fields.Notes: Bandits' Roost; a Danish-born police reporter whose book moved Theodore Roosevelt to close the police lodging houses.
fields.Description: He used magnesium flash powder to photograph New York tenements for How the Other Half Lives.
fields.Captions: Bandits' Roost, 59 1/2 Mulberry Street, 1888 | Street Arabs in the Area of Mulberry Street, c. 1889

fields.Title: Jeff Wall
fields.Notes: His A Sudden Gust of Wind (after Hokusai) restages a Hokusai print; a founder of the Vancouver School.
fields.Description: The Vancouver artist who stages large photographs and shows them in lightboxes, as in Dead Troops Talk.
fields.Captions: Dead Troops Talk, 1992 | Portrait of Jeff Wall

fields.Title: André Kertész
fields.Notes: His Distortions used funhouse mirrors; Cartier-Bresson said that all of them owed him something.
fields.Description: The Hungarian photographer of a dancer contorted on a studio sofa in Satiric Dancer.
fields.Captions: Satiric Dancer, 1926 | André Kertész in 1975

fields.Title: Bernd and Hilla Becher
fields.Notes: Teachers of Andreas Gursky, Thomas Struth, and Thomas Ruff at the Düsseldorf Academy; they won the Golden Lion for sculpture at the 1990 Venice Biennale.
fields.Description: The German couple who photographed water towers and blast furnaces head-on, in grids they called typologies.
fields.Captions: Water Towers, 1974–2009 | Bernd (centre) and Hilla Becher (right)

fields.Title: Nicéphore Niépce
fields.Notes: The exposure took hours or days, so sunlight falls on both sides of the courtyard; he partnered with Louis Daguerre in 1829 and died four years later.
fields.Description: The French inventor who made the oldest surviving camera photograph, a view from an upstairs window of his estate near Chalon-sur-Saône, by heliography on a pewter plate coated with bitumen of Judea.
fields.Captions: View from the Window at Le Gras, c. 1826–1827, in Helmut Gernsheim's 1952 enhancement | The original plate, Harry Ransom Center, Austin | One of his cameras, c. 1820–1830

fields.Title: Auguste and Louis Lumière
fields.Notes: Their photographic-plate factory paid for the Cinématographe, with which they launched cinema in 1895.
fields.Description: The brothers from Lyon whose Autochrome plates, coated with grains of potato starch dyed red, green, and violet, were the first practical colour photography, sold from 1907.
fields.Captions: An autochrome still life, 1912–1920 | The Pont du Change, Lyon, on a Lumière autochrome plate, 1935 | Auguste and Louis Lumière, c. 1895

fields.Title: George Eastman
fields.Notes: He also supplied Thomas Edison with the flexible film that made motion pictures possible; his Rochester mansion is now a museum of photography.
fields.Description: The American who founded Kodak, sold the first roll-film camera in 1888 with the slogan “You press the button, we do the rest”, and put photography in every hand with the one-dollar Brownie.
fields.Captions: George Eastman, 1917 | Eastman as a young man

fields.Title: Edwin Land
fields.Notes: His daughter asked why she could not see a photograph at once; Ansel Adams advised the company, and the SX-70 of 1972 made the format iconic.
fields.Description: The American inventor of cheap polarizing filters who founded Polaroid and in 1948 sold the first instant camera, which developed a print within a minute.
fields.Captions: Edwin Land presenting a Polaroid camera, 1971

fields.Title: Harold Edgerton
fields.Notes: He also developed night aerial photography for the Second World War and side-scan sonar, which he used with Jacques Cousteau to find shipwrecks.
fields.Description: The MIT electrical engineer, nicknamed “Papa Flash”, whose stroboscopic flashes froze a milk drop's splash crown and a bullet passing through an apple.
fields.Captions: Milk Drop Coronet, 1957 | Harold Edgerton with his cameras, 1963
